books.title: The 5 Love Languages
books.author: Gary Chapman
books.description: A simple framework for understanding how different people give and receive love.
ideas: People feel love differently

Gary Chapman noticed that couples often love each other deeply yet feel unloved, because they express love in different ways. He described five love languages: words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service and physical touch. Most people have one or two that matter most. Someone who longs for quality time may barely notice a gift; someone who values acts of service may feel cherished when you take out the bins. Today: think about which love language you speak most naturally, and which one makes you feel most loved.
Speak their language, not yours

We tend to show love the way we'd like to receive it. If you feel loved through words, you might write long messages, while your partner, who values acts of service, wishes you'd simply help with the washing up. Chapman encourages learning the other person's language and speaking it, even if it doesn't come naturally. Today: ask someone close to you what makes them feel most appreciated, and do one small thing in that language this week.
Keep the love tank full

Chapman uses the image of a love tank: when people feel loved in their own language, the tank fills, and they handle stress, disagreements and hard days much better. When it runs empty, small irritations become big fights. Small daily gestures, a kind word, ten minutes of attention or a hug, keep it topped up. Today: do one small thing to fill the love tank of someone you care about, before any problem arises.
Love is a choice

The early rush of infatuation fades in every relationship, often within a couple of years. Chapman argues that lasting love isn't a feeling that happens to us but a choice we make every day: choosing to care for someone in ways that matter to them. That choice can rekindle feelings, not just follow them. Today: choose one act of love for a partner, friend or family member that you'll do whether or not you feel like it.

books.title: Attached
books.author: Amir Levine & Rachel Heller
books.description: How attachment theory explains the way we behave in romantic relationships.
ideas: Three attachment styles

Attachment theory, described by Amir Levine and Rachel Heller, suggests that adults fall into roughly three styles in relationships. Secure people feel comfortable with closeness and trust easily. Anxious people crave closeness and worry about losing it. Avoidant people value independence highly and tend to pull away when things get too close. Knowing your style, and your partner's, can explain patterns that otherwise feel mysterious. Today: think about how you react when a partner or close friend goes quiet for a while. What does that reveal about your style?
Needing others isn't weakness

Many of us were taught that needing others is a weakness. Levine and Heller argue the opposite: depending on a partner is part of being human, and secure relationships actually make people more independent, not less. When you know someone has your back, you feel braver exploring the world. Today: let someone you trust help you with something, without apologising for needing it.
The anxious-avoidant trap

Anxious and avoidant people often attract each other, Levine and Heller observe, and then trigger each other's fears. The anxious partner reaches for closeness, the avoidant partner pulls back, which makes the anxious partner reach harder. The cycle can feel like passion but is often painful. Recognising it is the first step to breaking it. Today: if you see this pattern in a relationship, name it gently with your partner, without blame.
Effective communication

Saying clearly and calmly what you need, "I feel better when we text during the day", isn't needy; it's effective. Levine and Heller suggest that this kind of open communication quickly shows you who is willing and able to meet your needs. A good partner will respond with care; someone who mocks or ignores you is giving you important information. Today: express one need clearly to someone close to you, and notice how they respond.

books.title: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
books.author: John M. Gottman & Nan Silver
books.description: A relationship researcher's evidence-based guide to what makes couples last.
ideas: The four horsemen

John Gottman, who has studied thousands of couples, identified four behaviours that strongly predict break-ups: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. He called them the four horsemen. Contempt, treating your partner as beneath you through sarcasm, eye-rolling and mockery, is the most damaging. The good news is that each has an antidote, like gentle complaints instead of criticism and appreciation instead of contempt. Today: notice if any of the four horsemen show up in your next disagreement, and choose the softer alternative.
Turn toward bids

Partners constantly make small bids for attention: "Look at that bird", "Guess what happened at work?", a hand on the shoulder. Gottman found that couples who stay together turn toward these bids far more often, by responding with interest even briefly, while couples heading for trouble tend to ignore or dismiss them. These tiny moments build or erode connection over time. Today: notice the small bids people around you make, and respond warmly to as many as you can.
Love maps

Strong couples, Gottman found, know each other's worlds in detail: their worries, their friends, their dreams and their stresses this week. He calls this a love map. Maps go out of date as lives change, so they need updating with curious questions. Couples with detailed love maps cope better with difficult times. Today: ask your partner or a close friend an open question about something you don't know about their life right now.
Five to one

In stable couples, Gottman observed roughly five positive interactions for every negative one, even during conflict. Positive doesn't have to mean grand; it can be a joke, a touch, a nod or a moment of agreement. Kindness doesn't need to be dramatic, just frequent. A relationship with plenty of small positives can absorb the occasional argument. Today: add a few small positive moments to your interactions with someone close, like thanks, compliments or humour.
Some problems are permanent

Gottman found that many disagreements in relationships never fully go away. They come from deep differences in personality or values, like neatness, money or how social to be. Successful couples don't solve these perpetual problems; they learn to talk about them with humour, acceptance and understanding, instead of getting stuck in gridlock. Today: think of a recurring disagreement in one of your relationships, and approach it with curiosity about the other person's view rather than a goal of winning.

books.title: The Art of Loving
books.author: Erich Fromm
books.description: A psychologist argues that love is a skill to be learned, not a feeling we fall into.
ideas: Love is an art

We often think of love as something we fall into, a matter of luck and finding the right person. Erich Fromm argued that love is an art, like music or painting: it requires knowledge, practice, patience and effort. We spend a lot of energy on being lovable and very little on learning how to love. Today: think of one way to practise loving better, such as listening more carefully, being more patient or showing more appreciation, and practise it this week.
Love is active

For Fromm, love isn't primarily about receiving; it's about giving: care, responsibility, respect and knowledge of the other person. Giving, in this sense, isn't sacrifice but an expression of strength and aliveness. Love is something we do, not just something we feel. Today: do one active act of love for someone, like taking care of something for them, learning more about their world or showing respect for their choices.
Mature love keeps two people whole

Immature love says, "I love you because I need you." Mature love says, "I need you because I love you." Fromm described mature love as a union that preserves each person's individuality and integrity. Two whole people choose each other, rather than two halves clinging together. Today: reflect on one relationship and ask whether it lets both people grow, or whether one of you is shrinking to fit.
Self-love isn't selfishness

Fromm insisted that loving yourself isn't selfishness. Selfish people, he argued, often don't love themselves at all; they're anxious and empty. Genuine self-respect and care for your own growth are the ground from which you can love others well. You can't give what you don't have. Today: do one thing that shows care for yourself, like rest, a healthy meal or setting a boundary, without feeling guilty about it.

books.title: The Good Life
books.author: Robert Waldinger & Marc Schulz
books.description: Lessons from the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has followed lives for over 80 years.
ideas: Relationships keep us healthy

The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed hundreds of people for more than eighty years. Robert Waldinger and Marc Schulz, its current directors, report a clear finding: the quality of people's relationships predicted their health and happiness in old age better than wealth, fame or even cholesterol levels. People who felt connected at fifty were healthier at eighty. Today: think about which relationships nourish you most, and plan time with one of those people this week.
Loneliness is a health risk

Chronic loneliness isn't just painful; it's a real health risk, linked to poorer sleep, weaker immunity and shorter lives. The researchers note that you can feel lonely in a crowd and connected when alone; what matters is the quality of our connections, not the number. Social connection deserves as much attention as diet and exercise. Today: reach out to someone you haven't spoken to in a while, just to say you were thinking of them.
Social fitness

Waldinger and Schulz suggest thinking of social fitness like physical fitness. Relationships need regular exercise: checking in, making time, showing interest and working through conflicts. Neglected, they slowly weaken. It's easy to assume friendships will take care of themselves, but they rarely do. Today: do a quick social fitness check. Which relationships have you neglected lately, and what's one small step to strengthen one of them?
Small moments matter

Not all connection needs to be deep. Brief, warm interactions, a chat with a neighbour, a joke with a barista or a friendly word to a colleague, boost mood and sense of belonging more than people expect. The study's authors point out that these small moments add up across a life. Today: start a short, friendly conversation with someone you usually just pass by.
